story_text.value:
I built a website that makes you hear the voices in your head. They will complete your thoughts, in all the ways they might have unfolded, with your own voice. Everything runs locally in your browser.

I wanted the experience to be 1) local 2) realtime and 3) with voice cloning. Under the hood it’s VAD -> STT -> LLM -> TTS, respectively: - Silero - Parakeet CTC 0.6B - LFM2.5-350 ⁃ Pocket TTS

Ofc, they're not technically your thoughts. I finetuned the LLM on Simone Weil’s and Albert Camus’s personal notebooks. It is a small model, dumb in a weird fun way. You can also finetune it on your own notes or messages, and the experience with both your voice and some of your thought-pieces is a bit uncanny. Here’s the repo if you’d like to try: https://github.com/vidalmaxime/voices-in-your-head

story_text.value:
I was having intermittent issues with my ISP after switching and was looking for something that would let me easily trend downtimes, speed tests, and latency, but the existing projects out there (speedtest-tracker, myspeed, netcheck, etc.) lacked a few things I needed.

I gradually put together my own, it's simple to install and supports Linux, macOS, Windows, and Docker.

Interactive demo with sample data: https://demo.pingularity.dev/

- Install from https://pingularity.dev then open http://localhost:9000/, local network accessible, password protectable.

- Single-binary, no dependencies, self-hosted, no telemetry.

- Scheduled Ookla and iperf speed tests with a wide array of settings.

- Charts for visualizing download, upload, ping, jitter, and bufferbloat over time. Outage heatmap, live latency and DNS sampling.

- Uptime tracking with alerts and notifications. Webhooks with native ntfy and heartbeat.

- Manage retention, backups, or delete individual runs.

- Prometheus/Grafana with importable dashboard and alert rules.

- Customizable, change colours, disable stuff you don't want, remove chart tiles you don't care about.

- MIT license, https://github.com/pingular/pingularity

- I used Claude Code and Codex extensively throughout.

title.value: Show HN: Pingularity – scheduled Ookla/iperf3 speedtest dashboard, outage alerts

story_text.value:
Hello HN!

I built Worktable as an open-source, file-based workspace for you and your agents to create docs, plans, and build small tools.

For example, you ask an agent to compare hosting options for your next side project, save the research notes, and build a calculator where you can adjust traffic and storage assumptions yourself.

As a backstory, I run my Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw on a server at home and was consistently frustrated with the experience of trying to review/edit docs, share context between them, switch to other new agents, and more.

In the last few months, it has become what all my daily work depends on so I decided to make a product and release it for others to use.

What’s included:

- Markdown, richtext, HTML, structured records as YAML

- A built-in runtime and data API for HTML dashboards, calculators, planners, etc

- Comments and version history

- MCP connections to local, self-hosted or Worktable Cloud

- Threads for you and your agents + a dedicated OpenClaw plugin for automatic replies (Hermes coming soon)

- Plain files in regular folders. Same workspace format and export/import across local, self-hosted and cloud.

Free local/self-hosted, AGPL. Cloud is optional.

Try it with your agents. I’d love to learn what you do with it and what gets in the way.

Website: https://worktable.dev

Github: https://github.com/worktable/worktable-dev

story_text.value:
I started experimenting with LLMs and decided I wanted to create a fitness app. My first thought was an app that disabled Google Pay every time my phone detected I was within 50m of a McDonald's.

However, I quickly pivoted like a true founder to create an app that addressed a personal issue of mine.

On Android, if you have a bunch of apps and fitness monitors from different manufacturers, very few of them all talk to each other. Your data is scattered across different apps or double counted. However, most data sources write to Health Connect.

Hamilton is a dashboard of your Health Connect data with a homepage that shows your key metrics at a glance. Your choice of data source is flexible to avoid double counting, and you can overlay and offset metrics on charts to view correlations and track progress over time.

I named the app after my dog, who occasionally fetches things and is responsible for my daily step count.

Below is an FAQ, and to avoid confusion I have helpfully labelled my responses [APP] or [DOG].

FAQ

1. Is Hamilton any good?

[APP] I think so - I use it daily.

[DOG] He is the absolute BEST BOY EVER

2. How much does Hamilton cost?

[APP] £3.59 (or local equivalent). I priced it to be approximately the same as a latte, which is my standard unit of measurement for impulse purchases.

[DOG] DO NOT REMIND ME. He was a lockdown puppy and I bought him at the top of the market (He's still worth every penny though)

3. Is Hamilton vibe-coded?

[APP] 100% yes, but human-designed to fit my needs.

[DOG] He wants to create an app called Rate my Vet, with ratings dependent on how they take his temperature.

4. Is that unsafe? Will Hamilton delete data on my phone?

[APP] Everything is a read-only view on Health Connect, and the app has no internet permission. It can't delete your Health Connect data and it can't transmit data.

[DOG] No, but my cat jumped on my keyboard when I was in the middle of typing an insightful LinkedIn post and made me send RUBBISH to my THOUSANDS (20) of followers

5. Is Hamilton active in the background?

[APP] It fetches your data hourly from Health Connect if granted background access, and it works with Android battery saving rules.

[DOG] He's active in the background of my Zoom calls, mostly licking his genitals

6. Is Hamilton tested?

[APP] I've been using it daily and testing and refining it for months. I realise just typing this sentence means someone will find a critical bug the first time they run it and I will look like a FOOL.

[DOG] Only for tapeworm and parvo virus.

7. Do you eat your own dog food?

[APP] I use it every day to show my steps, body comp, workout sessions etc

[DOG] He does, but he would far rather eat whatever it is I have on my plate.

8. Does Hamilton show all your data?

[APP] 30+ metrics, everything except blood sugar and reproductive health

[DOG] The only data he gets is from sniffing lamp posts

9. What units does Hamilton use?

[APP] Metric, Imperial, and you can also configure per metric group to match the strange mix we have in the UK. No furlongs though.

[DOG] Approximately 6 urinations per 20m walked

10. Does Hamilton have any recurring costs?

[APP] I hate apps with subscriptions, and no internet permission means no backend costs so the app is paid once

[DOG] Vets are crooks, is all I will say on this.

11. Has Hamilton won any prizes?

[APP] Not yet

[DOG] Second in the Waggiest Tail Category at the Weald of Kent Ploughing Match. He was ROBBED.

12. Are the metrics on the Play Store yours?

[APP] Absolutely not. I have 5% body fat, do 20,000 steps a day and have a resting heart rate of 12.

[DOG] Yes

13. Where can I see Hamilton?

[APP] https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.gads.hamil...

[DOG] https://hamiltonapp.github.io/HamiltonApp/dog.html

title.value: Show HN: Hamilton – a no-internet Android health dashboard, named after my dog

story_text.value:
archive.aero is a free viewer for historical FAA sectional charts. Drag the timeline to see the charts in effect on that date. It's about 7,600 chart sheets stitched into one mosaic per edition. The scans come from the National Archives, the FAA, and charts contributed by the public. It's built on GDAL and PMTiles, so there is no tile server or backend. The browser reads tiles straight from Cloudflare R2 with range requests.

I'm a student pilot in North Texas and I always wanted a "ForeFlight time machine" to see what changed between editions. The gaps are at https://archive.aero/contribute (mostly 1970 to 2005) if you have old charts and would like to send them to be scanned.

story_text.value:
Hello! I built this static tool to generate wavy backgrounds for posts, socials and landing pages and decided to share it for free for anyone looking for the same.

This tool uses three.js/canvas rather than svg: a full-screen quad and a fragment shader which makes for soft shadows, smoother blurs and glass effects. Hit the randomize button to get a good shape + colour combination, optionally tweak using the vector tool, save designs to local storage and export to image or video.

What's the point? I started out thinking this would be something "easy" and that I could build in about an hour but turns out it does take a bit more effort to make it "look good". You can use the backgrounds for content or an over-engineered colour picker or just chill with it in fullscreen mode.

Screenshot: https://cdn.subworkflow.ai/marketing/wave-by-subworkflow-scr...

Enjoy!

title.value: Show HN: Wave – Layered gradient wave backgrounds using Three.js and shaders
